Large Load Customer Onboarding Process

From a Business Development perspective, onboarding a large-load customer – such
as a hyperscale data center, industrial facility, or manufacturing plant – is a multi-phase
process that can range from approximately 6 months for smaller projects with available
capacity to several years for gigawatt-scale facilities requiring major transmission,
generation, or substation investments. To manage grid capacity efficiently and prevent
speculative applications from clogging engineering bandwidth, the onboarding
framework pairs technical studies with formal readiness gates, queue management
protocols, and proactive supply chain strategies.

Phase 1: Qualification & Initial Screening

The process begins with the execution of a non-disclosure agreement (NDA) and an
initial qualification discussion to understand the customer's proposed location,
anticipated load, load ramp schedule, desired in-service date, reliability requirements,
renewable energy objectives, and long-term expansion plans. During this phase,
Business Development serves as the primary customer interface and coordinates
internally with Planning, Engineering, Regulatory, Legal, Finance, Construction, and
Operations to evaluate potential service options.

To advance to formal review, the customer must satisfy initial qualification requirements
by submitting a complete Large Load Interconnection Study application, required study
deposits, and documentation verifying project viability (such as proof of site control).
EPE then performs an initial screening assessment to determine whether existing
transmission, generation, and distribution infrastructure can accommodate the
requested load and to identify potential constraints. This preliminary assessment
focuses on available capacity at the proposed point of service, high-level transmission
requirements, substation considerations, generation sufficiency, and potential schedule
risks. Completed within several weeks, this review establishes whether more detailed
studies are warranted.

Phase 2: System Impact Study (SIS) & Queue Mechanics

If the project satisfies initial readiness thresholds, EPE assigns a formal queue position
and initiates a detailed System Impact Study (SIS). For regions or substations facing
multiple competing load requests, EPE applies queue management or cluster study
methodologies to model cumulative grid impacts and allocate shared network upgrade
costs fairly.

This phase typically requires several months and evaluates the customer’s impact on
the electric system under a variety of operating conditions. The study assesses

transmission loading, substation capacity, voltage performance, short-circuit impacts,
reliability criteria, generation adequacy, contingency performance, and potential NERC
compliance considerations. In parallel, power supply options – including green tariff
availability, clean energy procurement, or co-located generation/storage – are
evaluated. The objective is to identify all transmission, generation, distribution,
protection, and operational upgrades necessary to reliably serve the requested load
while maintaining system reliability for existing customers. For large customers,
multiple study iterations may be required as load forecasts, site plans, and infrastructure
assumptions evolve, yielding preliminary cost estimates for required upgrades.

Phase 3: Facilities Study & Long-Lead Supply Chain Management

Once required upgrades are identified and the customer satisfies Readiness Gate 2
(confirming project scope and study funding), EPE may perform a Facilities Study. This
phase translates high-level recommendations from the System Impact Study into a
detailed engineering scope, refined cost estimates (+/- 10–15%), and conceptual
construction schedules. The Facilities Study identifies specific transmission lines,
substations, transformers, breakers, protection equipment, communications
infrastructure, generation resources, and right-of-way requirements.

Because major infrastructure components – such as high-voltage transformers and
specialized switchgear – currently face extended lead times exceeding 2 to 3 years,
supply chain risks are proactively managed during this stage. Where necessary, EPE
and the customer may negotiate Long-Lead Procurement Agreements (LLPAs) to order
critical, long-lead equipment prior to full contract execution. Environmental reviews,
permitting, and land acquisition activities also begin during this phase for projects
requiring new corridors or substation expansions.

Phase 4: Commercial Negotiations & Contract Execution

While technical studies are underway, Business Development leads commercial
negotiations with the customer to ensure terms progress in parallel with technical
modelling. These discussions focus on execution of an Energy Services Agreement
(ESA) and address:

   Contract demand levels, phasing, and enforced load-ramp schedules.
   Temporary service arrangements and service commencement dates.
   Credit support, study cost reimbursements, and customer-funded infrastructure
    mechanisms.
   Minimum take-or-pay commitments, rate structures, and green tariff participation.
   Operational flexibility, curtailment provisions, and long-term expansion rights.
Legal, Regulatory, Finance, and Planning teams participate extensively throughout the
process to ensure the proposed commercial structure aligns with regulatory
requirements and EPE’s long-term system planning objectives. Following technical
study completion and commercial agreement, the parties execute the ESA. The
customer then posts required credit support (such as letters of credit or parental
guarantees), deposits, or construction advances to protect ratepayers against stranded-

asset risk. Necessary regulatory filings, environmental approvals, rights-of-way grants,
and internal governance approvals are finalized at this stage.

Phase 5: Project Execution, Construction & Energization

The final phase involves project execution, procurement, construction, testing, and
energization. EPE's Engineering, Construction, Operations, and Planning teams
oversee implementation of all required infrastructure upgrades and coordinate outage
sequencing to maintain grid reliability. Simultaneously, Business Development
maintains regular communication with the customer regarding milestones, schedule
tracking, and supply chain timelines.

Once all system upgrades are complete, field testing and relay protection validations
are signed off, and operational requirements have been satisfied, the customer’s load is
energized according to their agreed-upon ramp schedule. Business Development
remains engaged throughout the life of the customer relationship to coordinate future
load additions, ESA amendments, renewable energy procurement initiatives, and
subsequent project expansion phases.

TIEC 1-2:

    Referring to Exhibit JS-1

    a. Please explain whether EPE intends to include existing customers under this new tariff.

        If so, please explain why.

    b. Please explain why EPE did not include a Termination Fee in the tariff other than in case

        of a default.

    c. Please explain what factors would EPE consider when exercising its "reasonable

        discretion" in accepting an irrevocable and unconditional guarantee from the ultimate

        parent or corporate affiliate of the Customer.

    d. Please explain why EPE chose 75 MW as the appropriate threshold to qualify as a new

        very large load in EPE' s Texas retail jurisdiction.

    e. Please provide EPE's analysis supporting the proposed 20-year Initial Contract Term. In

        responding, please explain how the proposed 20-year Initial Contract Term ensures that

        new large load customers pay for the costs incurred to serve these loads.




                                                                                                   7
                                                               SOAH DOCKET NO. 473-26-24718
                                                                     PUC DOCKET NO. 59611
                                                                    TIEC's 1st, Q. No. TIEC 1-2
                                                                                     Page 2 of 2

RESPONSE:

     a. No existing customers currently qualify for service on the filed Schedule No. HLFLP

        tariff.

     b. EPE interprets a Termination Fee to imply the customer has a right to terminate the

        contract for convenience.        Termination for convenience is largely a financial

        determination for the customer, but could have significant system implications for EPE.

        Therefore, EPE did not include a termination fee in cases other than default.

     c. The “reasonable discretion” language is provided for flexibility in applying the security

        provisions of the proposed tariff, recognizing that significant difference may exist in the

        financial and corporate structure of eligible customers. EPE has not yet identified

        specific factors that would be considered, but in general EPE would assess the financial

        risk of accepting an irrevocable and unconditional guarantee from the ultimate parent or

        corporate affiliate of the Customer, such as the financial wherewithal of the parent or

        affiliate and the business history of the parent or corporate affiliate.

     d. EPE chose 75 MW as the threshold consistent with Senate Bill 6.

     e. EPE’s assessment is that 20-years is at the maximum length that prospective customers

        will accept, and which provides substantial assurance of recovery of capital investments

        associated with serving new large load. The more critical element for assuring the large

        load customers pay for costs incurred to serve the load is cost allocation and the

        ratemaking process.

TIEC 1-4:

     Would a customer still be required to take service under the tariff in the event that a 75 MW

     (or larger) customer self-supplied all, or part, of its generation behind-the-meter, such that

     its net load is less than 75 MW? Please explain your response.



RESPONSE:

     Yes, if the configuration of behind-the-meter generation was such that EPE would be

     expected to supply retail load requirements in the event of a customer generation outage.

         parent or corporate affiliate of the Customer.

     d. Please explain why EPE chose 75 MW as the appropriate threshold to qualify as a new

         very large load in EPE' s Texas retail jurisdiction.

     e. Please provide EPE's analysis supporting the proposed 20-year Initial Contract Term. In

         responding, please explain how the proposed 20-year Initial Contract Term ensures that

         new large load customers pay for the costs incurred to serve these loads.

RESPONSE:

     a. No existing customers currently qualify for service on the filed Schedule No. HLFLP

            tariff.

     b. EPE interprets a Termination Fee to imply the customer has a right to terminate the

            contract for convenience.        Termination for convenience is largely a financial

            determination for the customer, but could have significant system implications for EPE.

            Therefore, EPE did not include a termination fee in cases other than default.

     c.     The "reasonable discretion" language is provided for flexibility in applying the security

            provisions of the proposed tariff, recognizing that significant difference may exist in the

            financial and corporate structure of eligible customers.        EPE has not yet identified

            specific factors that would be considered, but in general EPE would assess the financial

            risk of accepting an irrevocable and unconditional guarantee from the ultimate parent or

            corporate affiliate of the Customer, such as the financial wherewithal of the parent or

            affiliate and the business history of the parent or corporate affiliate.

     d. EPE chose 75 MW as the threshold consistent with Senate Bill 6.

     e. EPE' s assessment is that 20-years is at the maximum length that prospective customers

            will accept, and which provides substantial assurance of recovery of capital investments

            associated with serving new large load. The more critical element for assuring the large

            load customers pay for costs incurred to serve the load is cost allocation and the

            ratemaking process.
